title: What expenditure is made of, and why a bigger body spends more

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Daily energy expenditure is made of three components, and they are not equal in size.

Resting energy expenditure (REE), from section 1, is the energy spent at rest. It is usually the largest of the three. The basal metabolic rate (BMR), from section 3, is not a fourth part. It is resting expenditure measured under set conditions: lying down, after a fast, in a room neither warm nor cold.

The thermic effect of food is the energy spent digesting, absorbing and processing what was eaten. Intake in this book is counted as metabolizable energy, not net metabolizable energy (Book 0, E2). So the cost of digestion is counted once, here, as expenditure.

Physical activity expenditure is the energy spent moving, whether as deliberate exercise or as the ordinary movement of a day.

Resting expenditure depends mainly on age, sex, body size and body composition. Physical activity expenditure depends on how much the body moves, in proportion to its weight. The thermic effect of food depends on what was eaten.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Every day, a body spends energy on three different kinds of work, and it does not spend the same amount on each.

Much of it goes on staying alive, doing nothing else. That is resting expenditure, and it is usually the biggest of the three. It is bigger in a bigger body, because more tissue means more of that background work. A person with more fat-free mass spends more at rest, whether or not they move at all that day.

A smaller share goes on the meal itself. Protein takes more effort to process than carbohydrate, and carbohydrate takes more than fat. This is the smallest of the three shares.

The rest goes on movement: everything from a deliberate workout to walking to the bus. Carry more weight through the same walk and it costs more.

A bigger body spends more, mostly because resting expenditure and movement both scale with size.

blocks.alt: A straight line through three points: 1 at 55 kg, about 1.55 at 85 kg and about 1.73 at 95 kg, the cost of the same activity relative to the 55 kg patient.
blocks.caption: If the cost of an activity is in proportion to body weight, as Hall and Guo (2017) put it, the same walk, or any activity that carries the body, costs the 95 kg patient 95/55, about 1.73 times what it costs the 55 kg patient. After losing ten kilograms, at 85 kg, it costs about 1.55 times: less, for the same activity.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Two patients come to the same clinic on the same day, both adults, both sedentary. One weighs 55 kilograms. The other weighs 95 kilograms and carries more fat-free mass than the first.

Ask which of them has the higher daily energy expenditure, before checking anything.

Open the review, Hall and Guo 2017, at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5568065/, and search for linearly related.

Across a wide range of weights, REE is linearly related to both fat-free mass and body fat, such that the elevated REE with obesity is generally in line with what is expected for the body weight and composition.

So the heavier patient’s resting expenditure is expected to be higher. Fat-free mass counts for more of resting expenditure than body fat does, though both add to it.

Now search the same page for proportion to overall body weight.

The energy expended in physical activities is determined by their duration and intensity in proportion to overall body weight.

Now imagine the heavier patient loses ten kilograms over the following year, some of it fat-free mass along with the fat. Search the same page for declines with weight loss.

physical activity energy expenditure declines with weight loss unless its quantity or intensity increases to compensate.

A smaller body doing the same daily activities spends less doing them. That is not a failure of anything.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
“Bigger body, more expenditure” holds for resting and activity expenditure. It does not hold for the thermic effect of food, which follows what was eaten.

The pattern describes what is generally expected for a given body weight and composition.

points.html: Daily expenditure is not one thing. It is resting expenditure, usually the largest share; the thermic effect of food, the smallest; and physical activity expenditure.

Resting expenditure rises with both fat-free mass and body fat. A person with more body fat generally has more fat-free mass too. So do not assume a person with obesity has a slow metabolism. The source reports the opposite. Their resting expenditure is generally higher in total than a leaner person’s, in line with their larger body.

Both resting expenditure and physical activity expenditure scale with body size. The energy it takes to keep a person at a steady weight is their maintenance requirement. It is set by that weight. So it does not hold once their weight has changed, and their fat-free mass with it. Expect it to fall as their weight falls.
Knowing the three components does not give you a patient’s requirement. Use them to check what any computed requirement has left out.

blocks.prompt: A colleague says a patient with obesity must have a slow metabolism. Open Hall and Guo 2017 at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5568065/ and search for Contrary to popular belief. Say what that paragraph shows, and what it does not.
blocks.answer:
It shows the colleague has the direction wrong. People with obesity generally have a higher absolute REE, not a lower one. Fat-free mass is elevated in obesity along with body fat, and REE is linearly related to both.

It does not show that metabolism is fast for the body’s size. The paragraph says the elevated REE is “generally in line with what is expected for the body weight and composition”. So it is higher because the body is bigger, not because it spends more than its size predicts.

It also says “generally”. It does not tell you this patient’s REE. Only a measurement would.
